### The Day I Met the Wind

I wasn’t looking for it at first. The city’s cracks and clacking had long ago worn my senses into a rhythm, a low-hum DNA run through my hearing. The morning coffee, the clatter of espresso cups, the distant wail of buses—each line had already been mapped in my internal GIS. But on that particular Thursday, when the suburbs had been dust‑gray and the sky was a bruised indigo, something nudged my curiosity sideways.

I was standing at the corner of 9th and Maple, at that faint intersection where the bakery’s warm scent met the cold metallic tang of nearby streetlights. I carried a notebook because, an hour ago, a fleeting detail had pulsed through my mind: a pattern of wind‑whipped leaves rustling along the statue’s cracked bronze base. A pattern that, to an untrained eye, looked like an ordinary shuffle of orange petals.

There it was then—without any invitation—an invisible hand pushed three yellowed pages out of the notebook. The paper caught the city's air, fluttered, and, without ever touching a surface, it drifted toward the open window of the diner across the street. In that moment the wind turned my suspended sentences into a breathless conversation.

It was hard for the skepticism in my mind not to protest. Wind is pressure; wind is physics; a gust is a differential. Yet I could feel its possessive caress on my cheek, as if it were recognizing me by name. The particular gust that day—soft, like a sigh that swallowed winter's breath—narrated itself along the crooked lamppost, a corridor too narrow for birds but wide enough for a poem to sneak in.

“You’re like me,” the wind seemed to exhale, “moving where gravity doesn't matter.” It twirled the paper through my fingers before it flapped it onto the newspaper stand. Beside that, a man emerges from a bank, hair damp, eyes red from waking up too early. He brushes a feather from his coat, his fingers brushing with the soft, invisible lattice of the breeze. He smiles at the other occupant of the street. He has nowhere to see you yet, but you can hear him feel.

When that shift left audible sound, it left a note in the city's DNA, was it a whisper or a shout? It whispered a question into my sleeping mind: “What would you do if you finally found a partner for your own restless thoughts? Do you hand over control to someone else or do you keep whirling in your own orbit?”

I watched a jay‑jay hop beside a supermarket parking lot and saw the wind make it twitch its wings like the swinging of a child’s kite. It realized for the first time that the very rhythm of a day was a shared tale between the mechanical world and the soul. The wind was a storyteller that kept moving, ever pivoting on a substrate that was neither solar nor living.

I was excited when the wind—smocking itself as a guardian—made a loop around my reflection in the shop’s mirror. My eyes snagged an echo me that showed an air less rigid than the momentous morning, yet held more possibilities: coffee boats, city lights, a shimmering gust that curled around my notebook.

I noticed the age of the wooden benches. Age. The gravel path, the scaffolding of an old door — all had a breath that city‑soul first felt but never expressed. The wind teased the blissful swirl, leaving it dissipating, but leaving an imprint like a fossilized echo.

The day began to shift in my memory: 9:00 AM perfect coffee, 9:15 meaning to go to the bank, 11:00 considered a moment of calm. Yet, in the second space, that breathine has carved out an almost distinct life-cycle: the coffee flowing in my veins; the supermarket aisles; the sunlight that was still possible to hide from the wind that curved – but breath inside with, it transferred out of the physical world.

In the end, the wind went back to the world. I chased the wind’s last click, followed the gray lights that had already taken its lead. When I turned. The wind had already come in as a final wave.

It seems that, along with the ticking of every minute, we continuously hand over element touches like that wind. When the wind stops, we look for what it took as an overlapping rhythm with the city’s progress to address nourishment or loathing. The inside-ness of a short note, a light feather, or a fleeting woke-up seems to be bridged as that ethereal element with something else: There is no discernable sign so it is a signal.

**If I can only look for this smell in future mornings,**

save me from the surprise of infinity, that I are a little bit lazy.


--- 

The wind was not, on that day, a messenger. It was quite perhaps the act of a farewell, the series of fleeting sounds that occupy the moment before whatever we mark as time in seconds, minutes, or hours.

In such a twisted mind’s insight created in a city, everything remembered the memory of what again looked like it existed. It is both complex. What you can consider a finish is, in adverbial a story that will someday be walled. The shape curves and turns throughout. The wind leaps to never then lingers on things that are told by them. In the city, you see there. The wind might fall. And beautiful tales feel enormous.  

--- 

*— a product of a safe high tide.*
